# raylib-starter

[![test](https://github.com/drsamonline/raylib-starter/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/drsamonline/raylib-starter/actions/workflows/test.yml)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-blue)](LICENSE)


![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)
**One C file, a fixed timestep, scenes, save and an ECS — on raylib.** The C answer to
`game-kit`: the same names, the same behaviour, and the same tests, on a 2.4 MB engine instead
of a browser.

Built for the 10 MB ceiling. A raylib game is one binary that runs on Windows, macOS, Linux,
the web (via Emscripten), Android and a Raspberry Pi.

## Use it

```bash
make              # the game        (needs raylib)
make test         # the suite       (needs only a C compiler)
make size         # fail if over 10 MB
make web          # the game in a browser (needs emsdk + raylib for wasm)
make wasm-core CC="zig cc"   # the core alone as wasm32, needs nothing installed
```

```c
gk_loop_init(&G.loop, 1.0 / 60.0);
gk_loop_tick(&G.loop, GetFrameTime(), loop_step, loop_draw, &G);   // fixed steps, then draw

gk_scenes_go(&G.scenes, "play", &G, NULL);                          // enter / exit / update / render
gk_save("progress.bin", &p, sizeof p);                              // magic + version + CRC32
gk_rng_seed(&G.rng, 12345);                                         // the same sequence as game-kit
```

## What is in it

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `gk_loop` | a fixed timestep: accumulator, a 0.25 s frame clamp, a 240-step cap, and an alpha for interpolation |
| `gk_scenes` | named scenes with `enter` / `exit` / `update` / `render`; an unknown name is refused rather than blanking the screen |
| `gk_input` | key down and pressed-this-frame, driven by the host — no engine types in the core |
| `gk_save` / `gk_load` | a struct on disk with a magic, a version and a CRC32, so a half-written save is caught, not loaded |
| `gk_ecs` | entities, component bags and systems over a bitmask; systems are handed the entity, so component access is O(1); `gk_ecs_queue_destroy` + `gk_ecs_flush` defer structural change out of a pass; fixed capacity, no allocation |
| `gk_rng` | mulberry32, **bit-identical to `game-kit`'s `rng()`** — verified in the tests |
| `gk_ease` / `gk_spring` / `gk_tween` | the eleven easing curves, the settle-time spring presets and a tween — **matching `motion-kit` to 1e-9** |
| `gk_camera` | world↔screen, follow with easing, zoom, deadzone, and bounds that keep the view inside the level |
| `gk_shake` | a camera kick as an elapsed-time effect: `make`/`start`/`step`/`running`, decaying to zero |
| `gk_machine` | named states, a transition table, enter/exit handlers; an event the table does not allow is refused, and names are copied into the machine. The demo's round uses one: warmup → live → finished |
| `gk_tween_chain` | several tweens stepped in order, with the overshoot carried so the chain keeps its total time |
| `gk_audio` | a thin wrapper over raylib's device: `init`/`load`/`play`/`stop`/`volume`/`playing`, volume clamped, calls routed and counted headless |
| `gk_tilemap` / `gk_move` | a grid of tiles with solid ids, and collide-and-slide: each axis swept and pushed back out, so a corner slides instead of sticking |
| `gk_atlas` / `gk_anim` / `gk_sprite_dst` | frame rectangles from a grid atlas, which frame is showing at time t, and where a world sprite lands on screen |
| `gk_tiles_visible` | the tiles a camera can see, as world rectangles, each with an optional atlas frame — a renderer walks the list, a test counts it |
| `gk_clampf`, `gk_lerp`, `gk_dist`, `gk_aabb`, `gk_circle_hit` | the maths `game-kit` exposes, same names |

### Targets

| target | needs | gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `make` | raylib + a C compiler | `gk`, the desktop game |
| `make test` | a C compiler | four suites, 432 assertions, headless, no display |
| `make size` | raylib | builds, then fails above 10 MB |
| `make web` | emsdk + raylib built for wasm | `web/gk.html` + `.js` + `.wasm` |
| `make wasm-core` | only a wasm32-capable compiler (`CC="zig cc"`) | `web/gk-core.wasm`, and its size |
| `make snake` | raylib + a C compiler | `snake`, the second game |
| `make test-snake` | a C compiler | 35 assertions for the second game |
| `make link-check` | a C compiler | both games' real `main()`, 120 frames headless |
| `make bench` | a C compiler | the ECS benchmark, at a 4096 entity cap |
| `make cross CC="zig cc"` | a cross-capable compiler | the core compiled for five other machines |
| `make size-real` | an unpacked raylib in `RAYLIB_DIR` | the real binary, gated at 10 MB |
| `ndk-build` in `android/` | Android NDK + raylib for Android | the game on Android |

The core is engine-free: `main.c` compiles with `-DGK_NO_MAIN` and then contains no raylib at
all. That is what makes it testable, and it is why the stub exists.

## A second game, to prove it is a starter

`examples/snake.c` includes `main.c` for the core only and brings its own rules, scenes and
save. That is the real test of whether this is a starter or just one game: if a second game
cannot reuse the machinery, the machinery is wrong.

```
make snake          # needs raylib
make test-snake     # needs only a C compiler
```

Its suite covers turning (and refusing a reversal), movement on the ticker, eating, the three
ways to die (wall, self, and the legal move into the cell the tail is leaving), food never
landing on the snake, and the best score round-tripping through the save file.

## The demo game

`main.c` is also a small game, so nothing here is a sketch: three scenes (title, play, over), a
player and six drifting motes that are all entities in the ECS, collection by AABB, a 30-second
round with a two-second warmup phase the scene draws "ready" through, and a best score saved to disk. The world is 1280×800 inside a 640×400 window, so the
camera has something to do: it follows the player and stops at the level edges. A ring of solid
tiles closes the world, and the player moves through `gk_move`, so it collides with the border
instead of bouncing off it — the motes still bounce, through the ECS system. It exercises every part of the core, which is why the
tests can drive the real game headless.

## Verified

```
make test
326 passed, 0 failed    (the demo game)
43 passed, 0 failed     (harvest)
28 passed, 0 failed     (audio)
35 passed, 0 failed     (snake)
```

What the suite covers, all headless — no engine, no window, no display:

- **the loop**: 60 steps from 60 frames, a 1 s frame clamped to 15 steps, a 0.25 s frame × 4
  giving 60 steps, the step cap holding and resetting the accumulator, alpha in `[0,1)`
- **the RNG**: five values from seed 12345 compared against `game-kit`'s JavaScript output to
  1e-12, seed 1 likewise, `rng_int` inside its bounds and reaching both ends, `rng_pick` in range
- **the motion**: all eleven easing curves checked at t = 0.25/0.5/0.75 against `motion-kit`'s
  JavaScript to 1e-9, the `smooth`/`snappy`/`bouncy` presets against its stiffness and damping,
  and each spring's curve at seven points — so a C game and a JS game move identically
- **scenes**: enter before exit ordering, routing of update and render, an unknown scene refused
- **save**: round-trip, a size mismatch, a foreign magic, a future version, one corrupted payload
  byte caught by the CRC, and an empty payload
- **ECS**: create/get/has/remove/destroy, systems matching only the entities that hold the
  components they name, systems in the order added, a full world refusing more entities
- **the tilemap**: world-to-tile flooring (including negatives), solid ids and the out-of-bounds
  rule, free movement exact, a wall stopping the box flush on each of four sides, a corner
  resolving both axes, sliding along a wall without losing the free axis, a block mid-sweep
  stopping the mover there rather than at the far wall, many 1px steps landing in exactly the
  same place as one big sweep, a closed world, and a null or zero-tile map moving freely
- **sprites and animation**: atlas rectangles for the first, a row end, a wrapped row, the last
  frame, a frame past the end and a negative frame; a degenerate and a null atlas; animation at
  t = 0, mid-frame, the wrap, a non-looping anim holding its last frame, fps 0 as a still, a
  sub-range wrapping inside itself and a reversed range; sprite destination through a camera at
  zoom 1 and 2, and with no camera at all
- **visible tiles**: a view covering the map sees all 15, a 32×16 view sees exactly 3, a view
  outside the map sees none, the capacity is respected, a null camera means the whole map, a null
  map means none, and zooming out shows more
- **camera shake**: start/step/running, offset within the amplitude, decay towards the end, stops exactly at the duration and clears the offset, a finished shake is inert, a negative step does not rewind, zero duration never runs, restart resets, null-safe
- **the camera**: world↔screen round-trips at zoom 1 and 2, the camera's own point lands at the
  viewport centre, follow closes the gap and arrives, speed 1 snaps and speed 0 does not move,
  bounds stop at half a viewport, zoomed in the view may travel further, a world smaller than the
  viewport centres instead of clamping, unbounded leaves the camera alone, a zero zoom is repaired
- **the game itself**: start goes to play, seven entities spawn, the clock advances, the player
  stays in the world, walking into a mote scores, the round ends on the clock, the best is kept

### What was and was not verified here

Being precise, because "it builds" is easy to overclaim:

- **The suite was compiled and run** with `zig cc` (Zig 0.17.1's bundled clang), the only C
  compiler available in the environment this was written in. 320 assertions, all passing.
- **The raylib-facing half compiles**: `main.c` with `main()`, the three render functions and the
  key mapping compiles against `stub/raylib.h`, which mirrors raylib 5.x signatures. That catches
  a wrong call, not a wrong engine.
- **The real raylib link was not performed here.** raylib needs X11 and GL headers that this
  environment does not have, so `make` and `make size` are the two things to run on your machine.
  `make` itself is not installed here either; the commands those targets wrap were run directly.
- **Size, measured against real raylib**: **902,424 bytes** stripped, linked against raylib 6.2's
  own `libraylib.a`. That is 881 KB, 11.6× under the 10 MB ceiling. `make size-real` and CI both
  check it.
- **The core compiles for wasm32**: `make wasm-core` produced a **1,351-byte** module at `-Os`
  with only the loop reachable, which is the portability proof that does not depend on
  Emscripten being installed. CI builds it on every push and fails above **64 KB**, so a
  retained libc or a creeping dependency is caught rather than noticed later.
- **Three suites run in CI**: 320 assertions for the demo game, 35 for snake and 28 for audio, under gcc on
  Ubuntu, in the same workflow that builds the wasm core.
- **Both games actually run, past the title**: `make link-check` links the real `main()` of each
  game (not the `GK_NO_MAIN` core) against the stub and runs it for 120 frames while the stub
  presses start and the arrows on a schedule. The log reads `gk frames=120 draws=2533` and
  `snake frames=120 draws=712` — the loop, the scene machine, the key mapping, the tile renderer
  and the sprite renderer all execute. A run that never left the title draws 480, so the draw
  count is asserted as a floor: it is what proves the play scene ran.
- **Capacities are compile-time**: `-DGK_MAX_ENTITIES=8` was run through the whole suite to
  prove the core adapts, and the default is 256.
- **The Emscripten build was not run here** — emsdk is not installable in the environment this
  was written in. `make web` and `web/shell.html` are the pieces to run with emsdk present.
- **What still is not proven**: that raylib itself draws. Everything above runs against the stub,
  so a wrong `DrawText` argument or a bad window flag would only show up on a machine with a GPU
  and a display.

## The same motion as the JS kits

`motion-kit` and this starter now share a vocabulary, and the tests hold them together:

| From motion-kit | In C | Agreement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 11 cubic-bezier curves | `gk_ease_named("out")` etc. | 1e-9 at three points each |
| `smooth(300)` stiffness / damping | `gk_smooth(300)` | 947.203211111 / 61.553333333 |
| `snappy(250)` | `gk_snappy(250)` | 1148.803236 / 54.2304 |
| `bouncy(280)` | `gk_bouncy(280)` | 662.878584183 / 36.045 |
| spring value at time t | `gk_spring_at(s, ms)` | 1e-9 across seven samples |
| `tween(from, to, dur, ease)` | `gk_tween(...)` | endpoints, midpoint, clamp |

The demo game uses it: collecting a mote eases a ring outward on the `out` curve, which is the
same curve the JS kits use for the same gesture.

## Warning-free

Every configuration compiles with `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` — the real build, the headless core,
the stub link, both games, both suites, the benchmark, the five cross targets and the wasm
module. Seven configurations, no warnings.

That took two things: a `GK_API` attribute on the core's entry points, because a single
translation unit that does not use all of them would warn about the rest; and a
`GK_EXPORT` guard around the wasm-only `export_name` attribute, which the other five targets
would otherwise reject.

## The real binary, measured

`make size-real` links the game against raylib 6.2's own `libraylib.a` — not the stub — and gates
the result. Measured on raylib 6.2, linux amd64:

| | bytes | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `libraylib.a` | 2,847,000 | the engine, static |
| game + engine, unstripped | 1,091,856 | dead code already dropped by the linker |
| game + engine, **stripped** | **905,752** | 885 KB, with camera, tilemap and sprites |
| 10 MB ceiling | 10,485,760 | **11.6× headroom** |

`tools/x11_stubs.c` carries six weak X11 symbols so this links on a machine with no X server;
on a machine with X11 the real symbols win and the binary runs. CI does this link and the gate
on every push, downloading raylib 6.2 itself.

Plain `make` needs the X11 development headers on Linux (raylib's static library references
`XConvertSelection` and five others). Where they are missing, `make size-real` is the target
that still links, because it carries the weak stubs.

## Portability, measured

The core has no engine in it, so it cross-compiles anywhere a C compiler runs. `make cross` does
this on every push:

| Target | Core object | Verified |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `aarch64-linux-musl` | 4,024 B | ✅ |
| `arm-linux-musleabihf` | 2,964 B | ✅ |
| `riscv64-linux-musl` | 4,736 B | ✅ |
| `x86_64-windows-gnu` | 9,986 B | ✅ |
| `aarch64-macos` | 3,048 B | ✅ |
| `wasm32-wasi-musl` | 1,351 B | ✅ |
| `*-linux-android` | — | ❌ needs bionic headers, i.e. the NDK |

Android is scaffolded in `android/` (`ndk-build`, two `.mk` files, a manifest note) and is
honestly marked as unbuilt here. ARM is what Android devices run, so the instruction selection
and float behaviour are already exercised by the two ARM rows; what is untested is bionic and
raylib's Android glue.

## Why not archetype storage

The textbook ECS groups entities by their component set and stores component data inline, so a
system walks only matching entities and the data is contiguous. It is genuinely faster — and
`make bench` measures whether that matters here:

| entities | scan ns/entity | archetype ns/entity | ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 256 | 8.1 | 0.46 | 17.7× |
| 1,024 | 17.2 | 0.47 | 36.6× |
| 4,096 | 8.9 | 2.18 | 4.1× |

The ratio is real and the absolute numbers are not: at the 256-entity default, one system run is
**2.1 µs** scanning against **0.12 µs** on archetypes — in a 16.6 ms frame at 60 fps that is
0.013% against 0.0007%. Archetype storage would cost component registration, inline storage and
archetype churn on every add and remove, to save a hundredth of a millisecond. It stays out, and
this table is here so the decision can be revisited if a game ever needs thousands of entities.

**The benchmark earned its keep anyway**: the first run showed 260 ns/entity, which turned out to
be a linear id lookup inside every component access — an O(n²) system. Systems now receive the
entity itself, `gk_ecs_comp(e, comp)` is O(1), and the same measurement dropped to 8.1 ns: a 30×
win on the shipped design.

## The stub

`stub/raylib.h` and `stub/raylib_stub.c` are the slice of raylib this starter uses: a virtual
clock, a scripted keyboard, and drawing that counts calls instead of drawing. Signatures match
raylib, so the same source compiles both ways, and adding a raylib call means adding it to the
stub too — the stub is the contract.

## Consumers

None yet — this is the first C kit in the fleet, written to be the starting point for the small
games. It is not wired into anything and changes no app.

# Remedy Finder ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) **An offline homeopathic repertory workbench — not another symptom search box.** [![Live app](https://img.shields.io/badge/live%20app-drsamonline.github.io%2Fremedy--finder-0f766e?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/remedy-finder/) [![Single file](https://img.shields.io/badge/single%20file-947%20KB-0d9488?style=flat-square)](dist/remedy-finder.html) [![No dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-0-2f6b3d?style=flat-square)](#architecture) [![Offline](https://img.shields.io/badge/offline-first-f6f4ef?style=flat-square)](#offline-and-install) [![Remedies](https://img.shields.io/badge/remedies-297-1a1a17?style=flat-square)](#the-data) [![Symptoms](https://img.shields.io/badge/symptoms-634-1a1a17?style=flat-square)](#the-data) [![Graded links](https://img.shields.io/badge/graded%20links-44%2C704-1a1a17?style=flat-square)](#the-data) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-a8701a?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) Desktop: picker and ranking side by side. Mobile: one thumb, bottom tabs, sheets.
--- ## Why this exists Most remedy finders are a search box over a list. A repertory is not a list — it is a weighted argument. Three things decide which remedy rises: **which symptoms you chose**, **how characteristic each one is**, and **how many remedies share it**. This app puts all three on screen at the same time. - The number beside every symptom is how many of the 178 remedies carry it. Rare symptoms discriminate; the picker tells you which are rare *before* you click. - Every symptom→remedy link carries the repertory's **grade 1–3**. Grade-3 links score higher, and ★ marks them. - Every remedy carries a **verbatim quotation** from a public-domain materia medica, labelled with book and year — so you can read the source, not a summary of it. ## What it does | | | |---|---| | **Repertorise** | 634 symptoms in 17 chapters, 5 quick packs, typo-tolerant search, live ranking in a Web Worker | | **Remedy search** | The search box also finds remedies by name, Latin name, clinical use and family — one click opens the monograph | | **Pin & watch** | Pin up to three remedies and change the symptoms around them; the pinned strip keeps showing each remedy’s live rank and score | | **Data packs** | Import a JSON pack to add remedies offline (validated against this app's symptom IDs, with a SHA-256 checksum so a tampered file is refused), or export the current data as a pack. Packs persist in IndexedDB and re-apply on load | | **Text search** | A third picker mode searches the materia medica itself — descriptions, both quoted sources and clinical uses — plus the repertory rubric paths, with highlighted snippets and one click to the monograph | | **Thermal tendency** | Per remedy: chilly / hot / mixed, derived from the thermal modality rubrics in the repertory (cold agg, warm agg, warm amel, cold bathing amel) with the evidence rubric and grade shown. 135 of 297 remedies have evidence; the rest say "not stated" | | **Remedy explorer** | Force-directed relationship map: labelled without overlap, node size by relationship count, kingdom and thermal filters, search, zoom and pan, hover to isolate a remedy's relationships. **Built for touch**: the layout is computed at the real canvas size, pinch to zoom, drag to pan, tap to open, refits on rotate | | **Sources & provenance** | In-app screen with live counts, quotations per source, licences and an explicit list of what the app does not do | | **Rare-only filter** | One toggle in Repertory mode keeps rubrics carried by three remedies or fewer — the characteristic material, not the fever rubric every remedy has | | **Full repertory** | A second picker mode: search **39,737 rubrics** from Repertorium Publicum by words — *fear of death*, *thirst small*, *worse consolation* — and repertorise directly on rubrics, alone or mixed with curated symptoms | | **Boards** | Keep several rubric sets inside one case — acute picture, constitutional picture, family history — switch between them, and compare their rankings side by side | | **Interface languages** | English, हिंदी and ગુજરાતી for the finder, results and tools. Repertory terms stay in English — they are the vocabulary of the source books | | **Symptom weight** | Mark each selected symptom strong (+) or doubtful (−); the ranking responds immediately, in both the worker and the main thread | | **Eliminative method** | Strike remedies out as you go; a struck strip lets you restore them. ## The data Every link is traceable. Nothing is generated by a language model at runtime, and gaps are reported rather than filled. | Layer | Source | Scale | |---|---|---| | Rubric grades | **Repertorium Publicum** (2008), Vladimir Polony — GPL v3 | 74,480 rubrics, 735,460 graded links | | Symptom → remedy links | Mapped to this app's 634 symptoms by exact name, synonym and checked alias | **44,710 links** across 297 remedies | | Materia medica text | Boericke 1906 · Allen 1916 · Kent 1904 · Clarke 1900 · Nash 1899 · Guernsey 1886 · Felter 1922 · Lippe 1866 · Cowperthwaite 1885 · Bell 1906 · Hale 1897 | 132 quotations | | Source verification | Each remedy's attributed sources checked against 12 full texts | 170 / 178 remedies | | Dataset | [`drsamonline/homoeopathic-materia-medica-repertory-json`](https://github.com/drsamonline/homoeopathic-materia-medica-repertory-json) — 72 books, 357,762 rubrics, 1,435,488 links | CC0 / GPL v3 | **Known limits, stated plainly** - Symptom→rubric matching is automated with a hand-checked alias table. That makes **your copy the only copy**, so there is an explicit durability layer: | Control | What it does | |---|---| | **Encrypted backup** | One file, AES‑256‑GCM with a PBKDF2 key (150,000 rounds). Four options, graded feedback, next question | | **Case comparison** | Two saved cases side by side: symptoms in both, added, dropped, and how the top twelve remedies moved between visits | | **Printable case sheet** | One page per case: patient header, complaint, notes, symptoms with chapter and frequency, top ten remedies with scores, and quotations for the top three, with the data edition and a disclaimer in the footer | | **Transfer codes** | Move one case, or several, between devices as an encrypted text code (PIN-protected) — copy it, save it as a file, or **show it as a QR** for a phone camera to read. No network, no account | | **Delta backup** | After a full backup, "Backup changes only" writes just the records that changed since — with deletions recorded too, and restored as a merge | | **Backup history** | The last ten backups, with date, record count and size, plus **how many records changed since the last backup**. | | **Encryption at rest** | Optional passphrase. Clinic cases, saved repertorisations and packs are stored as AES‑256‑GCM ciphertext; the key lives in memory only. A lock screen on start, auto-lock after 1/5/15 minutes idle, passphrase rotation with a reissued recovery key, and a "turn off" path that decrypts everything back to plain text. | | **Connection chip** | Top bar shows `offline-ready` / `offline` / `local file`, and updates as the connection changes. | Every saved repertorisation is stamped with the **data edition** it was scored against (`rp2008-297r-44710l`), so a case opened a year from now can say which dataset produced its ranking. ## Two builds, one codebase | | `remedy-finder.html` | `remedy-finder-full.html` | |---|---|---| | Size | 947 KB | 3.7 MB | | Curated symptoms (634) | yes | yes | | Full repertory search (39,737 rubrics) | no — the mode tells you so | yes | | Load time | instant | repertory index builds in ~0.3 s on first use | The repertory ships as a separate 1.9 MB file (`assets/repertory.js`) and is loaded **only when you open the Repertory picker**, so the default app stays small. The single-file "full" build simply inlines it. **What the 39,737 rubrics are:** every rubric in *Repertorium Publicum* that carries at least two of this app's 297 remedies, with the printed grade kept. Single-remedy rubrics are dropped — one remedy cannot discriminate — and 9,353 of the included rubrics carry exactly two, which makes them the sharpest material in the repertory. # The Repertory Desk

[![0 dependencies](docs/assets/badge-tests.svg)](docs/play/index.html)
[![70 volumes](docs/assets/badge-deps.svg)](docs/play/index.html)
[![offline yes](docs/assets/badge-offline.svg)](docs/play/index.html)
[![CC0 1.0](docs/assets/badge-licence.svg)](LICENSE)

**A quiet reading room for sixteen classical homoeopathic repertories, six materia
medicas and forty public-domain treatises** — 352,063 rubrics, 1,429,263 remedy
links (751,907 of them graded) and 5,392 sections of prose, read straight from the open
JSON library on GitHub. No account,
no server, no tracking, no build step.

**Live:** <https://drsamonline.github.io/repertory-reader/>  · 
**The reader:** <https://drsamonline.github.io/repertory-reader/play/>  · 
**The library:** <https://github.com/drsamonline/homoeopathic-materia-medica-repertory-json>

![The Repertory Desk](docs/assets/app-desktop.png)

## The treatises

The library also carries prose works as a **treatise**: no rubrics, no remedies. A
numbered treatise (the Organon) shows a § against each paragraph; a chaptered one shows
its chapter title instead. Each is a separate volume and none is merged with another.

Forty treatises, from the two Organons to Clarke's *Dictionary* in three volumes:

- **B. L. Hill**, *An Epitome of the Homeopathic Healing Art* (1861) — 50 sections

- **Edward Pollock Anshutz (ed.)**, *New, Old and Forgotten Remedies: Papers by Many Writers* (1900) — 125 sections

- **G. H. G. Jahr; A. Possart**, *Jahr's and Possart's New Manual of the Homoeopathic Materia Medica* (1853) — 409 sections
- **H. C. Allen**, *Keynotes and Characteristics with Comparisons of Some of the Leading Remedies of the Materia Medica* (1916) — 183 sections
- **Henry Newell Guernsey**, *The Application of the Principles and Practice of Homoeopathy to Obstetrics* (1866) — 77 sections
- **J. H. Pulte**, *The Homoeopathic Domestic Physician* (1855) — 223 sections
- **J. Henry Allen**, *The Chronic Miasms — Sycosis* (1908) — 23 sections

- **James Compton Burnett**, *The Curability of Cataract with Medicines* (1889) — 5 sections

- **James Tyler Kent**, *Lectures on Homoeopathic Materia Medica* (1904) — 251 sections
- **James Tyler Kent**, *Lesser Writings of James Tyler Kent* (1900) — 36 sections
- **James Tyler Kent**, *Clinical Cases* (1900) — 105 sections

- **John Henry Clarke**, *A Dictionary of Practical Materia Medica, Volume I (A–H)* (1900) — 435 sections
- **John Henry Clarke**, *A Dictionary of Practical Materia Medica, Volume II (I–P)* (1902) — 323 sections
- **John Henry Clarke**, *A Dictionary of Practical Materia Medica, Volume III (P–Z)* (1902) — 268 sections
- **John R. Kippax**, *A Hand-Book of Diseases of the Skin and Their Homoeopathic Treatment* (1890) — 138 sections
- **Joseph Laurie**, *The Homeopathic Guide for Family Use* (1870) — 89 sections
- **Joseph T. O'Connor (ed.)**, *The American Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia* (1883) — 580 sections
- **Margaret Lucy Tyler**, *Pointers to the Common Remedies (remedies by disease)* (1936) — 60 sections
- **Samuel Hahnemann**, *The Chronic Diseases: Their Specific Nature and Homoeopathic Treatment — the theoretical part* (1896) — 6 sections
- **Samuel Hahnemann R. E. Dudgeon**, *Organon of Medicine, fifth edition* (1849) — 294 sections
- **Samuel Hahnemann William Boericke**, *Organon of Medicine, sixth edition* (1922) — 291 sections
- **Samuel Hahnemann; translated from the latest German editions**, *Materia Medica Pura (A–I)* (1880) — 36 sections
- **Samuel Lilienthal**, *Homoeopathic Therapeutics* (1884) — 527 sections
- **T. C. Duncan**, *Diseases of Infants and Children, with Their Homoeopathic Treatment* (1879) — 165 sections
- **T. C. Duncan**, *Hand Book on the Diseases of the Heart and Their Homoeopathic Treatment* (1898) — 68 sections
- **Thomas Lindsley Bradford**, *The Life and Letters of Dr. Samuel Hahnemann* (1894) — 70 sections
- **Willis Alonzo Dewey**, *Essentials of Homoeopathic Materia Medica* (1894) — 6 sections
- **Willis Alonzo Dewey**, *Practical Homeopathic Therapeutics* (1900) — 102 sections

The two Organons are genuinely different books: 74 paragraphs are worded differently and
§292–§294 exist only in the fifth. Each paragraph carries the source it was read from and
the fraction of its 12-letter sequences found verbatim in OCR scans of that same edition,
so you can see for yourself that a paragraph is the book's text and not a reconstruction.

## What it is

A reader. It opens a volume on its own contents and shows each rubric the way the
book printed it — the symptom in the measure of the page, the remedies the book
sets beside it, and the printed grade marks where the source carries them. Every
remedy is a door: tap a chip to see the rubrics in that volume which list it.

It does not repertorise, score, rank, correct or complete anything. A repertory is
evidence; a reader that starts guessing stops being evidence.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Read** | A repertory opens chapter by chapter, in the printed order; a materia medica opens by remedy, with its portrait, clinical indications and symptoms grouped by chapter. Knerr's 43 chapters, Kent's 34, Gentry's A–Z; single-file volumes build their contents from the sections inside the file. |
| **Search** | Three scopes — the open chapter, the volume, then every volume already on your device. Remedy abbreviations and resolved names are searched too. |
| **Follow** | Remedy chips filter a volume to the rubrics that carry them; the rail can list a volume by its drugs instead of its chapters. |
| **Themes** | Paper, vellum, sage, slate, lampblack — remembered per device, with serif text at a measured line length. |
| **Offline** | Chapters are kept in IndexedDB and served by a service worker, so a second visit works with the connection off. HTML stays network-first, so a release is never hidden behind a stale cache. |
| **Fast** | No framework, no dependencies, no build. Rendering is windowed — a 13,000-rubric chapter paints sixty rows at a time. |

## This app is locked

`docs/play/` is hand-built and hand-maintained: no CI, no build workflow, no
bundler, and no packaging into an EXE, an APK or a Linux binary. It is not wired
into `app-builder` and no automation regenerates its markup or design. See
[LOCKED.md](LOCKED.md) — if a change cannot be made without a build step, the
change is wrong.

## Run it

```bash
git clone https://github.com/drsamonline/repertory-reader
cd repertory-reader/docs && python3 -m http.server 8000
# open http://localhost:8000/play/
```

By default the reader fetches the library from GitHub (jsDelivr, falling back to
raw.githubusercontent.com). To read a local mirror of the library instead — the
way this app was tested — put the library's files under your web root and add
`?lib=../lib/`:

```
play/?lib=../lib/
```

## The library

Every volume is public domain, transcribed from its own scan and published as
app-ready JSON with a QC report per book, plus a `catalog.json` manifest this
reader loads first. The library is versioned and rebuilt by scripts; this reader
is not.

Change it, then rebuild the release: ```bash npm install # installs terser (the only dev dependency) npm run build # src/retro-strike.html -> dist/retro-strike.min.html ``` --- ## 📦 Project structure ``` retro-strike/ ├── src/retro-strike.html # 📜 readable, commented source (edit this) ├── dist/retro-strike.min.html # 🎮 minified, playable release (~90 KB) ├── tools/build.mjs # 🔧 minifier (extracts + compresses src -> dist) ├── assets/ # 🎨 banner, logo, social preview, screenshots ├── docs/ # 📚 architecture, controls, performance, audit ├── .github/ # ⚙️ Pages workflow, issue & PR templates ├── package.json # 📦 build script (dev-only) ├── CHANGELOG.md · CONTRIBUTING.md · CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md · SECURITY.md └── LICENSE ``` **Source vs release:** `src/` is the human-readable single file you edit; `dist/` is the same game compressed for shipping. The GitHub Pages workflow publishes `dist/` so the repo is instantly playable online. --- ## 🛠️ Tech Built from scratch with **zero runtime dependencies** — only web-platform APIs: - **Renderer** — a hand-written software rasteriser on **Canvas 2D**: per-face camera-space projection, near-plane clipping and a painter's-algorithm depth sort. ---

A small, dependency-free visual-novel engine for the browser.
Plain JavaScript · one stylesheet · no build step · works offline

--- **Saga** is a visual-novel engine that runs from a static file server with nothing installed. It was built to make *Aethelgard — The Books*, and it is released on its own so you can make something else with it. > **The engine is MIT.** It ships no story and no artwork — you bring your own. > The *Aethelgard* games' artwork and story are a separate work, © Dr. Sohil > Momin, all rights reserved — free to play, not open source, and not contained > in this repository. See [Licence](#licence). ## ▶️ See it in action This engine was built to make **Aethelgard — The Books**, a visual novel in three books — 36 chapters and seven endings, all authored in plain `.scene` text files that this engine reads. Play it here: **[drsamonline.github.io/aethelgard-games/play/books/](https://drsamonline.github.io/aethelgard-games/play/books/)** It is one of two games in the *Aethelgard* world; the other is an RPG on a different engine, [drsamonline/Aethelgard-Engine](https://github.com/drsamonline/Aethelgard-Engine). Both live together in **[drsamonline/aethelgard-games](https://github.com/drsamonline/aethelgard-games)**. --- ## Contents - [See it in action](#-see-it-in-action) - [Run the engine](#run-the-engine) - [How to play](#how-to-play) - [Features](#features) - [Project layout](#project-layout) - [Write a chapter](#write-a-chapter) - [Art](#art) - [Mods](#mods) - [Making it yours](#making-it-yours) - [Documentation](#documentation) - [Contributing](#contributing) - [Licence](#licence) --- ## Run the engine The engine ships **code only** — no story, no art. To see it in action, play **[Aethelgard: The Books](https://drsamonline.github.io/aethelgard-games/play/books/)**, which is built on this engine. To build your own, see [Making it yours](#making-it-yours). The engine is served like any static site — it reads its scene files over http, so use a server (opening `index.html` by double-click will not work in most browsers): ```bash python3 -m http.server 8000 # open http://localhost:8000 ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) ``` No install, no build, no dependencies. Any static server works (`npx serve`, nginx, GitHub Pages — anything). ## How to play You read the story and make choices. That's the whole game — but there are a few things worth knowing before your first run. ### Controls | key | action | |---|---| | `Space` / `Enter` | advance dialogue (clicking the stage works too) | | `Tab` + `Enter` | move to a choice and pick it — every option is a real button | | `D` | open the **Diary** (people, places, lore, decisions, deeds) | | `B` | open the **Backlog** — scroll back through everything said | | `S` | save to localStorage (you can also export/import a JSON file) | | `Esc` | close the current panel | Mouse and touch work throughout; the layout is tested from 360×640 up. ### Choices and gates Some options show a requirement like `[Bonds 2]`. If you don't meet it, the option is shown **greyed out with the reason** — never hidden. You should always be able to see what you missed. ### The four axes and the endings Every choice secretly moves one of four counters: **Mercy**, **Truth**, **Bonds** or **Conviction**. They stay hidden while you play and are revealed in the epilogue. The ending is not a score — it is the *shape*: which axis led, and how far the four spread. Seven endings resolve from that shape, from *Dawn* to *Hollow*: | ending | the shape that earns it | |---|---| | Dawn | every axis high — nothing was sacrificed | | The Long Road | mercy carried the run | | The Weight | truth led, and its cost | | Ash | a balanced, ordinary run | | The Crown's Shadow | conviction led, without mercy | | Silence | never committed to anything | | Hollow | refused everything | The resolver lives in `js/endings.js` and is pure data — rewrite it freely. ### Tips - Read the Diary as you go — it fills itself and tells you who matters. - There is no wrong way to play; the seven endings are shapes, not grades. - Reaching the end of a chapter list without an ending still returns you to the title screen safely. ## Features | | | |---|---| | **Dialogue** | per-line speaker, ten expressions, a portrait that changes with the mood of the line | | **Choices** | branching, with stat gates shown greyed-out and their reason visible — never a hidden lock | | **Branches** | `@label` / `@goto`, so a choice can rejoin the main line | | **Four axes** | hidden counters that every choice moves; the ending is their *shape* | | **Seven endings** | resolved from which axis led and how far they spread | | **The Diary** | people, places, lore, decisions and deeds, filled as you play | | **Intro cards** | a character card the first time someone appears | | **Achievements** | declared in the script, unlocked in play | | **Save / export** | localStorage, plus export and import as a JSON file | | **Backlog** | scroll back through everything said | | **Music** | synthesised with Web Audio — no audio files at all | | **Mods** | drop a folder in `mods/`, it is found; five safety rules enforced | | **Mobile** | tested from 360×640 up | | **Accessibility** | full keyboard play, visible focus outlines, dialog semantics, `prefers-reduced-motion` honoured | ## Project layout ``` index.html the page css/style.css the look js/core.js state, save, settings, the four axes js/script.js the scene-script parser js/chars.js the cast and the regions <- YOUR DATA js/graphics.js sprite lookup js/music.js synthesised sound js/play.js the runner: dialogue, choices, diary, cards js/ui.js title, Diary, settings, endings js/mods.js the mod loader and its safety rules js/endings.js the axis shape and the ending resolver js/boot.js wiring scenes/ the story, as plain text <- YOU ADD THIS assets/sprites/ the art <- YOU ADD THIS docs/SCENE-FORMAT.md how to write a chapter ``` Everything marked **YOUR DATA** is meant to be replaced. The engine does not know anything about any particular story. ## Write a chapter A chapter is a plain text file, one instruction per line. Full reference in `docs/SCENE-FORMAT.md`. ``` @title The Demo — Chapter One @bg road @mood uneasy narrate A road at dusk. wanderer neutral "You're the Keeper of the hall, then." keeper warm "I am." choice * "Tell the truth." => truth+1, bonds+1 * [Bonds 2] "Say you knew her mother." => bonds+2, mercy+1 end @label after @mood calm keeper warm "Then come in. It's cold." ``` Then add one line to `scenes/manifest.js` and the chapter appears. ## Art The engine finds a portrait by name: ``` char.. -> _.webp, then .webp bg. -> bg_.webp ``` Ship no art and the game runs text-only — a missing portrait simply hides. The sprites in `assets/sprites/` here are **generated placeholders**, PolyForm Noncommercial-licensed like the engine. Replace them. Rebuild the index after adding art: ```bash python3 tools/make-sprite-index.py assets/sprites ``` ## Mods Drop a folder into `mods/` with a `mod.js`, add a line to `mods/mods.json`, and the engine finds it. Mods can add chapters, cast, regions, achievements, and can also *replace* existing entries. Five safety rules are enforced so a mod can never break a running game: 1. Every load is wrapped in try/catch — a broken mod cannot take the game down. 2. Structural mods apply at boot only, never mid-session. 3. `requiresMods` is honoured. 4. Two mods claiming the same `provides` conflict; the first wins, the second is refused **visibly**. 5. `loadAfter` orders mods deterministically. See `mods/README.md` for the full manifest format and the example mods. ## Making it yours The engine ships **no story**. To make a game you replace three things: | file | what to put in it | |---|---| | `js/chars.js` | your cast, your regions, `G.TITLE`, `G.SLUG`, `G.ACHIEVEMENTS` | | `scenes/` | your chapters, and a `manifest.js` listing them | | `assets/sprites/` | your art | Nothing else needs to change. The engine starts at whatever scene the manifest lists first, so it never needs to know your chapter ids. ## Documentation | document | about | |---|---| | `docs/SCENE-FORMAT.md` | the full scene-script reference | | `mods/README.md` | writing a mod, and the five safety rules | | `assets/sprites/README.md` | the art naming convention | | `CONTRIBUTING.md` | how to send changes to the engine | | `CHANGELOG.md` | release history | ## Contributing Read `CONTRIBUTING.md` first — the engine is meant to stay small, with no build step and no dependencies. Bug fixes, parser features inside the existing format, accessibility work and new mod hook points are all welcome. ## Support Free, offline, accountless — and staying that way. # Seance

<!-- shot:start -->

![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)

<!-- shot:end -->

[![live](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-online-22c55e)](https://drsamonline.github.io/seance/)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-blue)](LICENSE)
[![download](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/drsamonline/seance

**Sealed notes, opened once.** A message you can send that cannot be read twice: write it,
seal it with a passphrase, send the sealed text (or the `.txt` it downloads). The reader opens
it once on their own device — offline, no account — and the second attempt finds nothing.

Built with **crypto-kit** (AES-256-GCM) and **web-kit**.

## What it does

- **Seal:** a note + a passphrase → a sealed text (base64) you can paste anywhere.
- **Open:** paste the sealed text, or open the `.txt` you were sent, + the passphrase → the note.
- Authenticated encryption, so a wrong passphrase or altered text is rejected.
- Share the text and the passphrase **separately** — the text is useless alone.
- Everything happens on your device; nothing is sent anywhere.

## Run it

Open `docs/index.html`. That's the whole app — offline, from `file://` or Pages.
(It needs a **secure context** for Web Crypto: Pages is https, so the live site is
fine; some browsers restrict `file://`.)

## Structure

```
docs/index.html      the app
docs/web-kit.js      the shared runtime (drsamonline/web-kit)
```

## Honest limits

- A passphrase-sealed note is only as strong as the passphrase. Use a strong one.
- "Opened once" is remembered **on this device** — it is a courtesy, not
  enforcement; a determined reader can clear storage or open it elsewhere.
- Not a substitute for a vetted messaging app for anything truly sensitive.

**A machine-consumable knowledge base of the working methods behind the drsamonline projects.**

[![Landing page](https://img.shields.io/badge/landing%20page-open-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/skills/)
[![All projects](https://img.shields.io/badge/All%20projects-hub-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/)
[![Type: knowledge base](https://img.shields.io/badge/type-knowledge%20base-586069?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/skills/)
[![Format: Markdown + JSON](https://img.shields.io/badge/format-Markdown%20%2B%20JSON-586069?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/drsamonline/skills)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](LICENSE)

**Landing page:** <https://drsamonline.github.io/skills/>  ·  **All projects:** <https://drsamonline.github.io/>


This repository is a **machine-consumable knowledge base**. Each of the
projects under [`drsamonline`](https://github.com/drsamonline) has its working
*method* extracted into a reusable **skill**, so the same approach can be
reused, extended or branched from instead of being rediscovered.

## Conforms to the Agent Skills standard

This repository conforms to the **Agent Skills** standard — see
[agentskills.io/specification](https://agentskills.io/specification). That is a
claim we can make and did not, which is free credibility we had already earned.

Run `python3 validate.py` to check it. The validator enforces the standard's rules
for `name` and `description`, and the folder layout:

- **name** — 1-64 characters; lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens only; no
  leading, trailing or doubled hyphen; and equal to the folder name.
- **description** — 1-1024 characters, present.
- **layout** — a directory holding `SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter.

**What the claim does and does not mean.** We conform on the fields the standard
defines for `name` and `description`, and on the layout. We do **not** claim support
for every optional field: where one is unused it is *absent*, not present-and-empty,
which is what the standard allows. Anything more specific than that would be
inventing a compatibility we have not tested.

Non-directory entries are **skipped** rather than failed — this repository holds a
`.gitkeep`, and a validator that calls a placeholder file a broken skill is a
validator people stop running.

There are two kinds of skill:

- **Technique skills** — the cross-cutting methods that recur across many
  projects: the offline-first single-file web app, Android WebView packaging,
  the portable EXE launcher, the shared build/release workflow, the landing-page
  + SEO conventions, the auto-updating showcase hub, the open-data pipeline, the
  LAN single-server architecture, the theme-aware GitHub profile, optical file
  transfer, embedded-bundle feature gating, and safe repository cleanup.
- **Imported first-party skills** — 1,399 skills carry `upstream` provenance naming one of 61 public
  collections (Google, Anthropic, Vercel Labs, Hugging Face, Cloudflare, MiniMax, LambdaTest,
  Browser-ACT and others), deduplicated by topic and kept under their own licences. Fourteen more
  record several sources at once, and 31 record none because they arrived as an uploaded pack.
- **Vendored packs** — 22 skills imported unchanged from [ChrisTitusTech/titstack](https://github.com/ChrisTitusTech/titstack) (MIT): 19 `pack-*` category readings and the individual skills behind them. Each carries its own `LICENSE`.
- **Merged pack** — 43 skills record `merged_from` sources (188 source skills between them) from the
  owner's own collection. Duplicates were collapsed, near-duplicates merged into one skill per job
  with a routing table, and every source is preserved verbatim under `references/` inside the skill
  that absorbed it.
- **Project skills** — 110 skills name one or more drsamonline repositories in `source_repos`: what
  the project is, how it is built, how it is released, and what makes its workflow distinctive.

**Catalogue:** `1558` skills across 28 categories. The machine-readable index is [`catalog.json`](catalog.json); the landing page is <https://drsamonline.github.io/skills/>.

## Repository layout

```
README.md                     # this file — human index + how AIs consume the repo
llms.txt                      # short plain-text pointer for AI agents
catalog.json                  # machine-readable index of every skill
skills/<skill-id>/SKILL.md    # the skill itself (YAML front-matter + body)
skills/<skill-id>/meta.json   # machine-readable metadata for that skill
docs/                         # the landing page (its own sub-website)
```

Skill ids are lowercase-hyphenated and stable. Categories are a fixed set:

`web-app-patterns`, `android-packaging`, `windows-desktop`, `game-engine`, `data-and-schema`, `health-tools`, `landing-and-seo`, `ci-and-release`, `marketing`, `docs-and-planning`, `code-quality`, `linux-desktop`, `sysadmin-ops`, `media-design`, `frontend-ui`, `backend-services`, `testing-qa`, `security-audit`, `cloud-and-deploy`, `ai-and-ml`, `office-docs`, `engineering-workflow`, `notes-knowledge`, `mobile-apps`, `browser-automation`, `google-workspace`, `game-dev`, `product-management`.

## The skill format

### `SKILL.md`

YAML front-matter, then a body with five fixed sections.

```markdown
---
name: Human-readable skill name
description: One sentence — what the skill lets you do.
---

# Human-readable skill name

A short introduction.

## When to use
- ...

## Method
1. ...

## Key files / entry points
- ...

## Gotchas
- ...

## Source projects
- [repo](https://github.com/drsamonline/<repo>) — what it demonstrates.
```

### `meta.json`

```json
{
  "id": "lowercase-hyphenated-id",
  "name": "Human-readable skill name",
  "category": "one of the nine categories",
  "description": "One sentence.",
  "tags": ["..."],
  "source_repos": ["RepoName", "..."],
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "updated": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "source_snapshot": { "RepoName": "<latest commit SHA when derived>" },
  "subskills": ["related-skill-id", "..."]
}
```

`source_snapshot` maps each source repository to its latest commit SHA at the
time the skill was derived, so a consumer can tell whether the skill still
matches the code it describes.

## The catalogue

Every skill in the repository, by category, with the one line that tells you whether to open it. The id is the directory: `skills/<id>/SKILL.md` holds the method, `meta.json` its provenance, its licence and its upstream commit. Where a category has an index pack, the pack is named first — it is the routing table for that category.

## How an AI agent should consume this repo

1. Read **`catalog.json`** first — it is the single source of truth. It carries
   `generated`, `count`, `categories[]` and a `skills[]` array whose entries
   mirror each `meta.json`.
2. Pick the skill(s) you need by `id`, `category` or `tags`.
3. Read the matching **`skills/<id>/SKILL.md`** for the actual method.
4. To reuse a project's approach, follow its `source_repos` and, if the skill
   looks stale, compare `source_snapshot` against the repo's current HEAD.

A short pointer file for agents is also provided at [`llms.txt`](llms.txt), and
the same catalogue is rendered for humans at the [landing page](https://drsamonline.github.io/skills/).

## Keeping the catalogue current

The catalogue is refreshed by a weekly GitHub Actions workflow,
[`.github/workflows/refresh.yml`](.github/workflows/refresh.yml) (cron +
`workflow_dispatch`, `permissions: contents: write`). It performs the
**mechanical refresh only**: it re-reads the repository list from the GitHub
API, updates each skill's `meta.json` `updated` and `source_snapshot` fields
(and any changed source-repo metadata), regenerates `catalog.json`, and commits
only if something changed.

It does **not** rewrite the skill prose. That split is deliberate:

- **Mechanical refresh (automated)** — SHAs, dates, counts, `catalog.json`.
  Safe to run unattended every week.
- **Prose update (human/AI, separate)** — the `When to use`, `Method`, `Key
  files`, `Gotchas` and `Source projects` text. Rewriting a method from a diff
  is a judgement call, so it is never done by the scheduled workflow.

### Vendored third-party skills

The five `pack-*` skills and the seventeen skills they merge are imported from
[ChrisTitusTech/titstack](https://github.com/ChrisTitusTech/titstack) at commit
`b9b7fb0`, under the **MIT** licence (© 2026 titstack contributors). Each of
those directories carries the full MIT text as its own `LICENSE`, and each
`meta.json` records the upstream repo, path and commit. MIT content is
redistributed here with its notice intact; the repository's PolyForm
Noncommercial terms continue to apply to the drsamonline skills around it.

`source_repos` is left empty for those entries on purpose: they describe a
repository that is not part of `drsamonline`, so the weekly refresh workflow
must not try to resolve their commit SHAs. The pin lives in `upstream.commit`
instead, which the refresh does not touch.

### The merged pack

43 skills in this repository record `merged_from` sources — 188 source skills
between them. One such pass, on 2026-11-07, merged 64 skills uploaded as a
single archive from the owner's own collection. The archive held 85 entries: 70
distinct skills, 13 byte-identical duplicates of those, and two files that were
not skills at all (a Windows archiver and a probe-results folder), which were
dropped.

The merge is by **job**, not by name. Skills that solved the same problem from
different angles became one skill with a routing table; skills that merely
shared a topic stayed apart, because a skill that answers two unrelated
questions retrieves badly for both. Each merged skill keeps every source
verbatim in `references/<source>/`, including that source's `LICENSE` where it
shipped one, and its `meta.json` lists `merged_from` so nothing is silently
lost. `source_repos` is empty for these entries so the weekly refresh does not
try to resolve a SHA for a skill that has no upstream repository.

### The multi-repo import

1,399 skills carry `upstream` provenance naming one of 61 public skill
collections, at the commits recorded in each `meta.json`. The
import is a **deduplicated** one: where two repositories shipped the same topic
the fullest version is kept and the others are listed under *Upstream variants*
inside that skill, so nothing is silently dropped and no two entries claim the
same ground.

Licences are per skill, not per repository — `MIT` for most, `Apache-2.0` for
`google/skills` and `huggingface/skills`, each with its full text in that
directory's `LICENSE`. Two sources (`anthropics/skills`,
`vercel-labs/agent-skills`) publish **no licence file**; their skills are
included at this repository owner's explicit direction and carry a
`LICENSE-NOTICE.md` instead of a grant. Twenty-three skills were mined from the
aggregator collections to fill categories with thin first-party coverage; they
are marked `origin: third-party-aggregator` and their upstream attribution is
incomplete by nature.

`source_repos` is empty for every imported entry on purpose — the weekly refresh
workflow resolves SHAs against the `drsamonline` repo list, so a foreign repo
name there would be dropped on the next run. The pin lives in
`upstream.repo/path/commit`.

### The third import

1,013 more first-party skills from 45 repositories, deduplicated against everything
already here: 21 topics already had a fuller version in the catalogue, so the new
copy was recorded under *Upstream variants* instead of adding a second entry, and 6
existing entries were replaced because the new source was substantially fuller.
Four categories were added (`browser-automation`, `google-workspace`, `game-dev`,
`product-management`) and every index pack was regenerated, so a pack now covers
all members of its category rather than the batch it was born with.

Five listed repositories contributed nothing: `NeoLabHQ/sadd`, `NeoLabHQ/kaizen`,
`baskduf/codex-fable5`, `oliverb-io1902e8/agent-skills-collection` and
`testmu-ai/api-skill` do not exist at those URLs, and `agentskills/agentskills`
carries no `SKILL.md`. Four more are aggregators (`davila7/claude-code-templates`,
`ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills`, `alirezarezvani/claude-skills`,
`foryourhealth111-pixel/Vibe-Skills`); they were read for overlap but not bulk
imported.

New categories are listed compactly in this README: at this size the descriptions
belong in the pack tables and `catalog.json`, not in 1,000 more README rows.

### Pruning

The catalogue is not a mirror. After the imports it was cut back to what does
real work:

- **142 skills removed.** The four Anthropic office skills that reserve
  all rights (`docx`, `pdf`, `pptx`, `xlsx`); a placeholder template; two alias
  stubs that only pointed at another skill; and the product-internal CLI wrappers
  with no reusable method (`ctx-*`, `caveman-stats`, `caveman-compress`,
  `remotion-render`).
- **124 thin families merged into 12 skills.** The 81
  `nexu-io/html-anything` style specs (median body 266 bytes) became five style
  libraries grouped by what you are producing: deck, web page, dashboard, visual
  card, document. The 45 `googleworkspace/cli` `recipe-*` skills became six
  grouped recipe sets by service. The two `grilling` aliases folded into
  `grilling`. Every original id survives as a heading inside its merged skill, so
  nothing was lost, only indexed.

Everything kept is substantive: the median body across the catalogue is several
kilobytes, and each skill states a trigger, a method and the traps it hit.

# SMARTNOTE — SCHEDULER ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) **Notes that schedule themselves.** Write a note in plain English; it is classified, prioritised, dated and reminded. No folders, no date pickers, no category dropdowns. [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-dc2626?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) [![Status: in development](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-in%20development-dc2626?style=flat-square)](#status) [![Demo: none](https://img.shields.io/badge/demo-none%20%C2%B7%20needs%20a%20server-6b7280?style=flat-square)](#why-there-is-no-hosted-demo) [![Tests: vitest](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-vitest-16a34a?style=flat-square)](#run-it-locally) [![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-19-000?style=flat-square&logo=react&logoColor=61dafb)](package.json) [![Vite](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vite-000?style=flat-square&logo=vite&logoColor=ffd62e)](vite.config.ts) [![tRPC](https://img.shields.io/badge/tRPC-000?style=flat-square&logo=trpc&logoColor=fff)](client/src/lib/trpc.ts) [![Drizzle ORM](https://img.shields.io/badge/Drizzle%20ORM-000?style=flat-square&logo=drizzle&logoColor=C5F74F)](drizzle/schema.ts) [![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-000?style=flat-square&logo=typescript&logoColor=3178c6)](tsconfig.json) [![MySQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/MySQL-compatible-000?style=flat-square&logo=mysql&logoColor=4479A1)](drizzle.config.ts) **[Project page](https://drsamonline.github.io/smartnote-scheduler/)** · [Run it](#run-it-locally) · [Status](#status)
--- ## What it does | | | |---|---| | **Five categories, assigned for you** | Tasks, Deadlines, Schedule, Thoughts and Learning — chosen by the model, not by you. | | **Priority and dates from plain language** | Low / Medium / High, plus the date and time the note contains. | | **Reminders that survive a restart** | Due reminders are processed by a heartbeat endpoint, not an in-process timer. | | **Delivery you can audit** | Every push and email attempt is logged as `sent`, `failed` or `skipped`. A failure is visible, never silent. | | **Search, filters, stats** | Full-text search, category tabs, hide-completed, and totals for pending and overdue. | | **Your notes stay portable** | JSON backup and restore, plus CSV and Markdown export. | ## How it works 1. **Write it plainly** — one box: *“renew the insurance by Friday”*, *“standup tomorrow at 9am”*. 2. **It reads and files it** — one pass: category, priority, a title, and the date and time it found in your words. 3. **You get reminded** — the reminder is stored with the note and delivered by push, or by email when a webhook is configured.

**One card for the day.** Your date, one intention, one task, and a streak — and every card you
have written, listed underneath so you can open it again. Write on Monday, read it on Tuesday.
Offline, no accounts, no telemetry.

Built with **web-kit** and **Forge**.

## What it does

- Shows today's date.
- Lets you write **one intention** and **one task** for the day.
- Keeps a **streak** of consecutive days you filled it in.
- Remembers everything on your device; **Export** writes a CSV of every day.

## Run it

Open `docs/index.html` in a browser. That's the whole app — it works from
`file://`, offline.

## Build the EXE and APK

On every push, GitHub Actions builds a portable Windows EXE and a signed Android
APK (via the shared `app-builder` kit) and attaches them to the `app-latest`
release. See `.github/workflows/build-apps.yml`.

```
docs/index.html      the app
```

tokens-kit: # tokens-kit **Colour, size, shadow — and motion.** This kit absorbed `motion-kit` on 2026-11-12: the springs, easings and transition presets live here as `T.motion.*`, because a token set without its motion is half a design system. [![live](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-online-22c55e)](https://drsamonline.github.io/tokens-kit/) [![test](https://github.com/drsamonline/tokens-kit/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/drsamonline/tokens-kit/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-blue)](LICENSE) **The Lobe UI token set as data.** Zero dependencies. One file. 121 colour names, 187 colour values per mode, a 19-field size scale and the three elevations — generated from lobe-mygo's own token source so it cannot drift from it. ## Use it ```js var T = require("./tokens-kit.js"); // Node; in a browser it is window.Tokens T.light.BgContainer; // "#ffffff" T.dark.Text; // "#e6e6e6" T.mix(T.light.Fill, T.light.Text, 0.15); // a colour, premultiplied like the source T.shadow("modal", "dark"); // a CSS box-shadow string, ring included T.cssVars("light"); // { "--lobe-BgContainer": "#ffffff", ... } ``` ## Opt-in, always **This kit changes nothing on its own.** Importing it touches no element, no document, no stylesheet and no storage — the tests assert that the source contains no `document.`, no `window.` and no auto-apply. The only function that writes anything is `T.apply(el, mode)`, and it writes to exactly the element you hand it. That is deliberate. The drsamonline apps keep their own `design.css`, and the fleet is not being rebranded: adopting Lobe's palette is a decision made one app at a time, by you, or not at all. This kit makes the tokens *available*; it does not impose them. ## What it does - **121 colour names × 2 modes** — `BgBase`, `BgContainer`, `TextSecondary`, `PrimaryHover`, `ErrorFill`, the nine-step palettes and the rest, values straight from `@lobehub/ui` 6.15.2 - **187 colour values per mode** — the 121 named tokens plus the palette scales - **`T.mix(a, b, t)`** — the exact port of `theme.Mix`: premultiplied alpha, clamped `t`, so mixing a translucent token into an opaque one does not darken it - **`T.contrast(a, b)`** — WCAG relative luminance and ratio, compositing a translucent colour over a background first, because a ratio needs an opaque colour to mean anything - **`T.shadow(level, mode)`** — `modal`, `popover`, `tooltip`, each the layered shadow plus the one-pixel ring that stops a light card dissolving into a light page - **`T.scale`** — radii (4/6/8/12), control heights (18/27/36/45), font sizes (12–38), line width and strong weight - **`T.fillBorder(mode)` / `T.fillBorderStrong(mode)`** — the two derived border tokens, so a caller does not re-derive them - **`T.cssVars(mode, prefix)` / `T.cssText(mode)`** — the tokens as `--lobe-*` custom properties, ready for a stylesheet ## Generated, not typed `tokens-kit.js` holds the data inline because the kit has no build step. The block between the `@generated` markers is written only by the generator: ``` node scripts/gen-tokens.js # tokens.source.json -> the DATA block in tokens-kit.js ``` `tokens.source.json` is the extraction of lobe-mygo `pkg/theme/tokens_gen.go` and `pkg/theme/shadow.go` at commit `5b3ecde`, which is itself generated from `@lobehub/ui` 6.15.2. The API around the block is hand-written; regenerating is idempotent and touches nothing else. ## Verified ``` node test-node.js 55 passed, 0 failed ``` The tests check that all 121 names resolve in both modes, that light and dark actually differ, the parse/format round-trip, that `mix` is premultiplied rather than a naive channel average, that white-on-black is 21:1 and both body-text pairs clear AAA, that the shadow rings differ by mode, that the CSS variables number 209, and — the important one — that the kit never touches `document`, `window` or storage and never auto-applies. ## Consumers None, by design. No app in the fleet is modified by this kit or by this pass. `motion-kit` and the three component kits are built to be adopted deliberately; nothing is retrofitted. ## Support Free, offline, accountless — and staying that way. --- ## Why Forge ships offline, single-file apps with **no build step**. Every framework needs a bundler and a `node_modules`, so none can be used — but the useful part of a framework (signals, reactive effects, declarative DOM) fits in a couple of kilobytes. `ui-kit` is that part, tested, so every app stops hand-rolling it. ## What's in it | | | |---|---| | `signal(v)` | a value with subscribe/notify; call it to read and track | | `computed(fn)` | a derived signal — lazy, cached, re-derives when a dependency changes | | `effect(fn)` | re-runs when any signal it read changes; returns a disposer | | `h(tag, props, …)` | hyperscript — declarative DOM, no compiler | | `text(sig)` | a text node bound to a signal | | `list(items, key, render)` | a **keyed list** — the same node is reused for the same key across reorders | | `on` / `bus` | DOM events and a tiny event bus | | `router()` | a hash router; the route is a signal | | `bind(sig)` | two-way form binding, in one place | ## Usage ```js var UI = require("./ui-kit.js"); // Node; in a browser it is window.UI var count = UI.signal(0); var double = UI.computed(function () { return count() * 2; }); var app = UI.h("div", {}, UI.h("button", { onClick: function () { count.update(function (n) { return n + 1; }); } }, "+"), UI.text(function () { return "count " + count() + ", double " + double(); }) ); UI.mount(app, document.body); ``` ## The proof: TodoMVC `examples/todomvc.js` is **TodoMVC built on the kit** — add, toggle, edit (double-click), destroy, toggle-all, the three filters, clear-completed and the items-left count, with the hash driving the filter. # Weft-8 Classroom ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) **Nine exercises that teach how a computer actually works — on a real one.** [![Live exercises](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-the%20exercises-e8d48b?style=flat-square&labelColor=1c2b24)](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-classroom/) [![Test](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/weft8-classroom/test.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=tests&labelColor=1c2b24)](https://github.com/drsamonline/weft8-classroom/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![Build + deploy](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/weft8-classroom/build-apps.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=build&labelColor=1c2b24)](https://github.com/drsamonline/weft8-classroom/actions/workflows/build-apps.yml) [![Licence](https://img.shields.io/badge/licence-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-9fe0a8?style=flat-square&labelColor=1c2b24)](LICENSE) [![Built on the Loom](https://img.shields.io/badge/built%20on-the%20Loom%20(app--jacquard)-e8d48b?style=flat-square&labelColor=1c2b24)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard) [![For classrooms](https://img.shields.io/badge/classrooms-free%20to%20use-9fe0a8?style=flat-square&labelColor=1c2b24)](#for-teachers) [**Open the exercises →**](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-classroom/) · [Teacher's sheet](TEACHER.md)
![The exercises](docs/shot.png) A first lesson in how computers work, built on the **Weft-8** — the 8-bit machine from [Jacquard, the Loom](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard). Sixteen registers, four flags, twenty-seven instructions, and **no `if` statement**, so the student builds one. Every exercise starts **incomplete**. The machine runs, does something, and the class can see exactly what is missing — then the check names the register and the value that was expected. ## The nine exercises | # | Exercise | What it teaches | |---|---|---| | 1 | Put a number somewhere | `LDI` fills the accumulator, `MOV` moves it | | 2 | Add two numbers | what `ADD Ra, Rb` really means | | 3 | Double a number | `SHL` is multiply-by-two | | 4 | Count to ten | a loop needs a counter, a decrement and a branch | | 5 | Remember something | `STORE` and `LOAD` reach RAM at `0x80` | | 6 | Call a subroutine | `CALL` pushes, `RET` pops — and the code after the call proves you came back | | 7 | Decide something | `CMP` sets the flags, `JZ` branches: your first `if` | | 8 | Say something out loud | `OUT` hands a byte to a port | | 9 | Swap two registers | why a swap needs a third register — and why "just copy it" loses a value | ## For teachers [`TEACHER.md`](TEACHER.md) has the lesson plan, the answers in words, three things worth saying out loud, and a table of common mistakes with what they look like on screen and what to ask the student. Two properties make it usable in a real classroom: - **Offline, one file, no accounts.** A room with no internet and a decade-old laptop can run the whole lesson. There is nothing to install. - **No partial credit.** The machine has no partial answers, so a tick means the program is right — not that it looks right. ## Built on the Loom `docs/play/weft8.js` is the **Weft-8** from [app-jacquard](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard), byte for byte the same engine. A student who finishes these eight can open Jacquard, or the puzzle set in `app-weft-puzzles`, and it is the same computer. ## Test it ``` npm install node test-node.js # 72 assertions — the machine, every exercise, and the checks node tests/page-smoke.js # 10 assertions — the page, driven in jsdom ``` The suite asserts the three things a teaching pack must be able to promise: 1. **every exercise is solvable** — the shipped answer passes its own checks, on the real machine 2. **every starter is genuinely incomplete** — it must *fail*, or there is nothing to teach 3. **the checks bite** — subtracting instead of adding, forgetting to `LOAD` back, ending a subroutine with `HLT` instead of `RET`, and writing one byte when two were asked for are all caught, each with the message a teacher would give ## The Weft-8 family One machine, seven faces. Every one of these runs `weft8.js` from the Loom, byte for byte — learn it once and you have learned all seven. | | what it is | |---|---| | [the Loom](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-jacquard/) | the machine and its editor — where it all starts | | [Weft Puzzles](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-weft-puzzles/) | five puzzles solved in assembly, a robot on a grid | | [Clip Loom](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-clip-loom/) | clipboard programs you can read: strip, squeeze, wrap | | [Weft-8 on hardware](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-hardware/) | the same machine in C, three-way parity with the JS one | | [weft8-kit](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-kit/) | rules small enough to sign off | | **Weft-8 Classroom** (you are here) | eight exercises that teach how a computer works | | [Weft-8 beside x86 and ARM](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-compare/) | the same four jobs in three machines | ## Support | | | |---|---| | UPI (India) | `drsohilboi@ybl` — payee Dr Sohil Momin, open amount, or scan [the QR](docs/assets/upi-qr.svg) | | GitHub Sponsors | [github.com/sponsors/drsamonline](https://github.com/sponsors/drsamonline) | | Ko-fi | [ko-fi.com/matneo](https://ko-fi.com/matneo) | | PayPal | [paypal.me/drsohilmomin](https://paypal.me/drsohilmomin?locale.x=en_GB&country.x=IN) | | My books | [Amazon author store](https://www.amazon.com/stores/author/B08ZT331LY/allbooks?ccs_id=aed72b9f-71d9-41dc-adee-e9368a317acc) | | More apps | [drsamonline.github.io](https://drsamonline.github.io/) | | Email | [sohilmomin2000@gmail.com](mailto:sohilmomin2000@gmail.com) | ## Licence **PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0** · © 2026 Dr Sohil Momin. # Weft-8 beside x86 and ARM ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) **Which part is the computer, and which part is the language?** [![Live columns](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-three%20columns-2f6f4f?style=flat-square&labelColor=1e1f1c)](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-compare/) [![Test](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/weft8-compare/test.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=tests&labelColor=1e1f1c)](https://github.com/drsamonline/weft8-compare/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![Build + deploy](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/weft8-compare/build-apps.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=build&labelColor=1e1f1c)](https://github.com/drsamonline/weft8-compare/actions/workflows/build-apps.yml) [![Licence](https://img.shields.io/badge/licence-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-8c4a3b?style=flat-square&labelColor=1e1f1c)](LICENSE) [![Built on the Loom](https://img.shields.io/badge/built%20on-the%20Loom%20(app--jacquard)-2f5a8c?style=flat-square&labelColor=1e1f1c)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard) [**Open the three columns →**](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-compare/)
![Three columns](docs/shot.png) Five small jobs, written three times: for the **Weft-8** (the Loom's 8-bit machine), for **x86-64**, and for **AArch64**. Put them side by side and the answer to "what is a computer, really?" stops being abstract — load, add, compare, branch, store. Everything else is naming. ## The five jobs | Job | What it shows | |---|---| | **Add two numbers** | the Weft-8 must move a literal into a register first; the other two add one straight in | | **Sum 1 to 5** | x86 does it in two instructions, ARM in one, the Weft-8 in three — `SUB` sets flags but cannot branch | | **The greater of two** | a compare, a conditional branch, two paths that converge. Identical shape on all three | | **Remember, then recall** | the Weft-8 addresses memory with a literal byte; x86 and ARM compute an address from a frame or stack pointer | | **Multiply by four** | two shifts here, one wide instruction there — the same idea in a wider instruction | ## Honest about the columns The **Weft-8 column is executable**. The page runs it on the real machine, shows the registers afterwards, and the test suite asserts the result of every one of the four jobs. The **x86-64 and AArch64 columns are hand-written illustrations** — short, accurate in shape, and labelled as illustrations in the page and in the data. They are not compiler output, and they do not claim to be. A listing that pretends to be compiled when it was typed by hand would be exactly the sort of thing this whole estate exists to avoid. ## Built on the Loom The Weft-8 column is `docs/play/weft8.js` from [Jacquard (the Loom)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard) — byte for byte the same engine, the same one its 102 assertions cover. ## Run it Open `docs/index.html`, or the [live columns](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-compare/). ## Test it ``` npm install node test-node.js # 65 assertions — the four jobs and the honesty of the columns node tests/page-smoke.js # 9 assertions — the page, driven in jsdom ``` The suite asserts that every Weft-8 listing assembles, halts, fits the 128-byte ROM and leaves the expected register or memory value; that every job says what it is, what the machines share and what actually differs; and that **both illustration columns say they are illustrations** and contain real mnemonics rather than a comment pretending to be code. ## The Weft-8 family One machine, seven faces. Every one of these runs `weft8.js` from the Loom, byte for byte — learn it once and you have learned all seven. | | what it is | |---|---| | [the Loom](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-jacquard/) | the machine and its editor — where it all starts | | [Weft Puzzles](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-weft-puzzles/) | five puzzles solved in assembly, a robot on a grid | | [Clip Loom](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-clip-loom/) | clipboard programs you can read: strip, squeeze, wrap | | [Weft-8 on hardware](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-hardware/) | the same machine in C, three-way parity with the JS one | | [weft8-kit](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-kit/) | rules small enough to sign off | | [Weft-8 Classroom](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-classroom/) | eight exercises that teach how a computer works | | **Weft-8 beside x86 and ARM** (you are here) | the same four jobs in three machines | ## Support | | | |---|---| | UPI (India) | `drsohilboi@ybl` — payee Dr Sohil Momin, open amount, or scan [the QR](docs/assets/upi-qr.svg) | | GitHub Sponsors | [github.com/sponsors/drsamonline](https://github.com/sponsors/drsamonline) | | Ko-fi | [ko-fi.com/matneo](https://ko-fi.com/matneo) | | PayPal | [paypal.me/drsohilmomin](https://paypal.me/drsohilmomin?locale.x=en_GB&country.x=IN) | | My books | [Amazon author store](https://www.amazon.com/stores/author/B08ZT331LY/allbooks?ccs_id=aed72b9f-71d9-41dc-adee-e9368a317acc) | | More apps | [drsamonline.github.io](https://drsamonline.github.io/) | | Email | [sohilmomin2000@gmail.com](mailto:sohilmomin2000@gmail.com) | ## Licence **PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0** · © 2026 Dr Sohil Momin.
